q: Which fracture pattern is most consistent with non-accidental injury (NAI) rather than a single accidental event?
o: Multiple fractures in different anatomical regions, each at a different stage of healing
An isolated greenstick fracture of the distal radius in a 6-month-old puppy
A single transverse femoral fracture with a consistent history of being hit by a car
e: Multiple fractures at different stages of healing indicate injuries at different times, which raises concern for repeated inflicted trauma.

q: Subconjunctival and scleral haemorrhages in a cat without external facial trauma are most consistent with
o: a sudden rise in intracranial or intrathoracic pressure from shaking or choking.
hypertensive retinopathy from chronic kidney disease.
anterior uveitis secondary to FIP.
e: These are classic findings after shaking or choking, which raise pressure in the head and chest.

q: A dog has haemoabdomen, pale mucous membranes and tachycardia. Radiographs show free abdominal fluid and a poorly defined diaphragm. Which injury is most consistent with blunt NAI?
o: Bile peritonitis from a ruptured common bile duct
Ruptured spleen or liver and a diaphragmatic hernia from high-energy abdominal compression
Ruptured urinary bladder from urethral obstruction
e: Stomping or kicking can rupture abdominal organs and the diaphragm at the same time.

q: Which animal best fits the ASPCA NAI high-risk profile?
o: A 6-year-old spayed female Golden Retriever with an annual wellness visit and no injuries
A 4-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat, indoor only, with a normal examination
A 10-month-old intact male mixed-breed dog of 12 lb (5.4 kg) that cowers and urinates when the owner approaches
e: Young age, intact male, mixed breed, small size and fearful behaviour toward the owner are all risk factors.

q: An owner brings a dog with a femur fracture and says it fell off the couch yesterday. You also find a 3-week-old healing rib fracture and fresh bruising over the dorsal thorax. What is your obligation?
o: Accept the history, because couch falls can fracture the femur in small dogs.
Document all findings objectively, treat the animal and report to animal control or law enforcement.
Withhold treatment until law enforcement arrives and takes a statement.
e: Fractures at different healing stages with fresh bruising are incompatible with the stated history. Treat the animal, document, and report.

q: Why is the skull important to include in a full-body radiographic survey of an NAI suspect?
o: Skull radiographs are required by law in cruelty cases.
Dental radiographs are more sensitive and replace skull films.
Skull fractures may be occult and need significant force, so finding them strengthens the diagnosis.
e: Skull fractures need substantial force and are inconsistent with most accidents described by owners.

q: Damage to the claws or nail beds of a cat presented as a cruelty case is most suggestive of
o: onychomycosis from a chronic fungal infection.
dragging, restraint or direct trauma to the feet consistent with NAI.
self-mutilation from a compulsive disorder.
e: Nail bed avulsions, fractured claws or burns of the claw tips are recognised NAI findings.

q: An owner takes their dog to a different veterinary clinic at each visit and uses a different surname each time. Which NAI caretaker risk factor is this?
o: Financial difficulty, which requires the cheapest clinic each time
Practice shopping, to prevent detection of a pattern of repeated injuries
Seeking multiple opinions before agreeing to treatment
e: Using several practices with name discrepancies is a recognised risk factor consistent with concealing repeated injuries.

q: A 7-week-old kitten in a shelter has burns that a veterinarian attributes to microwave radiation. In a published case report of this injury, under which heading did the authors place it, and what does that imply for the veterinarian's actions?
o: Accidental household injury, so treatment of the burns is the only action required
Maltreatment, so the veterinarian should document and photograph the injuries, treat the burns and involve the authorities as in any suspected abuse case
A husbandry error by shelter staff, so the incident is handled through internal quality review only
e: The case report was indexed under burn management, forensics and maltreatment, so microwave injury in a kitten is handled as suspected non-accidental injury with forensic documentation.

q: A dog is found with a rope around its neck and forelimbs. The autopsy shows lesions compatible with strangulation, and the stomach contains food mixed with blackish microgranules. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Record strangulation as the cause of death, because a visible lethal mechanism makes further testing unnecessary
Complete toxicological testing of the stomach contents and organs, because several methods of killing can be used on the same animal
Skip toxicology, because poisoning would have caused obvious gross lesions in the organs
e: In a published case of 'overkilling', strangulation was confirmed histologically, but the stomach findings led to toxicology that identified poisoning as well. A visible cause of death does not exclude other lethal mechanisms.
